results.title: eToro and Alpaca Get SEC Staff Relief for Brokerage Accounts That Hold No Cash
results.description: eToro USA Securities and Alpaca Securities won no-action relief from US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) staff this week for accounts that hold no customer cash. The money sits at a bank or a money transmitter instead. The two letters set how much capital each firm needs and how customer money may move. eToro's US broker-dealer, which introduces accounts to a clearing firm, may run the model with minimum net capital of $5,000. Alpaca, which carries and clears accounts itself, keeps a minimum of $250,000 or 2% of aggregate debit items, whichever is greater. Both firms are expanding in the US. eToro agreed in August to buy US equities and options broker TradeZero for up to $231 million in cash , a deal it expects to close in the first half of 2027. Funding From Bank, Crypto and Remittance Accounts Lowenstein Sandler, the law firm that filed both requests, said the accounts can draw on customer bank, crypto or remittance accounts held with affiliated or third-party providers. It said the structure can ease foreign exchange conversion and help foreign customers reach US markets. Alpaca already sells US market access to brokers abroad. Indonesian broker Valbury began routing its clients' US stock orders to Alpaca in January . Dutch neobank bunq, which holds customer money under an EU banking license, filed for US broker-dealer registration in April 2025 with plans to add stock trading. How the Money Moves The outside account can be held at a bank or at a state-licensed money services business registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). Customers must open one as a condition of getting the brokerage account. In the example set out in eToro's request, a customer buying one $100 share also instructs the money transmitter to send $100 to the carrying firm. The share is credited when the trade settles one business day later. After a sale, the proceeds go back to the external account under a standing authorization the customer signs. Alpaca said it would send them before the close of the next business day. It also agreed to exchange reconciliation reports with the money transmitter daily. Alpaca, which raised $435 million in July, including debt from Kraken parent Payward and BMO , clears trades for its own customers and for brokers it serves. Raymond Lombardo, acting associate director in the SEC's Division of Trading and Markets, signed both letters. [#highlighted-links#] He wrote that the staff position was "based strictly on the facts and circumstances stated in your Letter." Customer agreements must say that money sent to the external account is not held in the brokerage account. It is therefore not protected by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC). Funds at the money transmitter may not be mixed with its own money. eToro and Alpaca must also check periodically that the bank or money transmitter keeps its licenses. What the Letters Leave Open The relief is a staff position, not a Commission rule. It covers the net capital rule in eToro's case and, for Alpaca, the customer protection rule's limits on moving credit balances out of an account. Alpaca's request leans on a 2014 staff FAQ, updated in 2020, which says a customer can authorize continuing transfers to an outside account with a single instruction. The staff said it took no view on other federal, state or foreign laws or on self-regulatory organization rules, and that the position can be modified or revoked. eToro's letter refers to an unnamed carrying firm, while its US disclosures name Apex Clearing as its clearing broker. Both firms will keep offering traditional accounts, according to the requests. Neither gives a launch date. eToro USA Securities began offering commission-free US stock trading in July 2020 , after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) approved its membership. This article was written by Damian Chmiel at www.financemagnates.com.

results.title: From Tantura to Naza: History Was Not Falsified, Nor Was Testimony Silenced by Dr Sania El-Husseini
results.description: The Israeli documentary Naza attracted considerable international media and political attention after winning the Venice Film Festival’s Special Jury Prize, despite not yet having reached the wider public. Following its screening at the festival, the film received a 25-minute standing ovation, an unusual occurrence at such events. The film runs for 80 minutes. Its Hebrew title, Naza, means “collateral damage” that is, the number of civilians expected to be killed or injured when a particular military strike is carried out. The documentary examines the system used to select targets, including the reliance on artificial intelligence during bombing operations in Gaza, and explains the mechanism by which the number of civilians expected to be killed or injured as a result of a strike is calculated in advance. The film draws on a three-year investigation and the testimonies of 24 people from within the Israeli military establishment, including soldiers and officers whose identities were concealed in the documentary. A similar documentary Tantura, released four years before Naza, did not generate the same level of media and political attention, despite the significance of the subject it addressed and the elements of overlap between the two films. Tantura was screened at the Sundance Film Festival in early 2022 and focused on the massacre that befell the village of Tantura, all traces of which subsequently disappeared after the Alexandroni Brigade took control of it in May 1948. The film drew its account from the thesis of University of Haifa researcher Teddy Katz who revisited the material on which his research was based. Katz conducted 140 hours of interviews with 135 Palestinian and Israeli witnesses, although he was subsequently attacked and his academic credibility challenged. Reports that the Israeli Ministry of Defence had concealed historical documents from the archives relating to the Nakba and the role of military operations in emptying Palestinian villages, some of which had already become available, helped spur the making of Tantura and a return to the documentation underlying Katz’s thesis. Following the film’s release, Haaretz published an investigation and called for a search for mass graves. The following year, Forensic Architecture drew on testimonies, documents, historical aerial photographs and other evidence to reconstruct the village digitally and identify sites believed likely to contain mass graves in the territories of 1948. Naza provoked a fierce reaction both internationally and within Israel following its screening, in contrast to Tantura, reflecting the change we are witnessing today in the aftermath of 7 October. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for the citizenship of the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Zor, to be revoked and accused them of treason. Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir also asked the public prosecutor’s office to investigate the possibility that classified information had been leaked to the filmmakers. By contrast, more than 1,500 filmmakers, intellectuals and public figures signed a statement expressing solidarity with the film’s directors. An article published in Haaretz called for Gaza to be opened to journalists, while another warned against targeting any Israeli who speaks about the crimes in Gaza. Both films document, through evidence, Israel’s policy of erasing the traces of Palestinians from their land. Tantura exposes how Israel erases Palestinian history from memory and the historical record, while Naza exposes some of the mechanisms through which the Palestinian presence is being diminished today. The Israeli government’s reaction to Naza also reveals its policy of erasing the traces of crimes and suppressing testimony against it. The directors of Tantura and Naza, Alon Schwarz, on the one hand, and Yuval Abraham and Rachel Zor, on the other, are comparable in terms of their standing, although the latter two have become more widely known following Naza. Schwarz directed Aida’s Secrets, which was screened at Canada’s Hot Docs documentary festival and won the Audience Award at Israel’s Docaviv documentary festival. Abraham and Zor were among the four directors of No Other Land, which won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature last year. Yet the events surrounding the emergence of Naza have ultimately given its directors greater media prominence and international recognition. Following the events of 7 October and Israel’s war on Gaza, and its extension into the settlers’ war in the West Bank, international reports began increasingly to focus on the term “erasure of the Palestinians”. International sanctions against settler practices in the West Bank also began to intensify, culminating today in a qualitative shift in the international response of a kind Israel has not faced before. Since 2024, international reports have increasingly drawn attention to Israeli policies aimed at erasing the traces of Palestinians from their homeland. In early October 2024, a United Nations report entitled Genocide as Colonial Erasure linked Gaza and the West Bank, including Jerusalem, to a long trajectory of displacement and replacement. In February of this year, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights issued a report raising concerns about ethnic cleansing in Gaza and the West Bank amid escalating violence against Palestinians, the systematic destruction of entire neighbourhoods, forced displacement and demographic transformation. Another report, issued by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in May, addressed unprecedented levels of killing, mass displacement and the intensification of Israeli control over Palestinian life and land in Gaza and the West Bank, including Jerusalem. In June, Amnesty International issued another report entitled Erasing Everything Palestinian, focusing on the ethnic cleansing of Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities in the West Bank. A Human Rights Watch report published in August concluded that settler violence was driving displacement, documenting the displacement of 117 Palestinian communities since the beginning of 2023 and highlighting the Israeli state’s material, financial and legal support for armed settlers. That same month, Haaretz revealed in a report that the Israeli military had formed and supported a number of armed militias operating inside Gaza that raided residential areas, opened fire, broke into and looted homes, and then set them ablaze, with the aim of driving Gazans from the areas in which they lived. This September, the same month in which Naza was screened, the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem issued a report entitled Israel’s Systematic Dismantling of Palestinian Collective Life in the West Bank, drawing on the testimonies of more than 2,000 Palestinians collected over three decades. The title of B’Tselem’s report perhaps recalls the systematic dismantling of Palestinian collective life in Palestine before and after 1948, in Gaza, and indeed within the territories of 1948 themselves. Palestinian society inside Israel is also subjected to a different form of violence, but one that serves the same objective of dismantling Palestinian collective life. More than 200 Palestinians are killed each year, particularly since 2023, as a result of crime and violence in Palestinian communities, while most of these crimes remain unresolved or are not pursued by the Israeli police. This stands in contrast to the situation in Jewish communities. A report published by Le Monde last August revealed how some Palestinian families have been forced to leave because of crime in their neighbourhoods. Human rights reports and international and even Israeli journalistic investigations have become increasingly explicit and forthright in exposing Israel’s crimes against the Palestinians and linking them to the objective of erasing the Palestinian presence in the West Bank and Gaza, as occurred nearly eight decades ago. The international response to Israel’s actions against the Palestinians has evolved and become more explicit. In 2024, the Netanyahu government faced a range of American, British, Canadian and European Union sanctions targeting settlers accused of violence, the displacement of Palestinians and the seizure of their property, as well as entities and organisations that support them. Although President Trump reversed these sanctions after taking office, such measures subsequently expanded among Western countries. This year, European countries have increasingly articulated their positions collectively. A joint official statement issued on 9 June 2026 by the foreign ministers of Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Norway and New Zealand confirmed that they had taken coordinated action, including sanctions and other measures, to hold extremist settlers accountable for violence against Palestinian civilians. The statement said that settlers “use violence to displace Palestinians”, that “settlement expansion and the establishment of outposts continue with the support and facilitation of the Government of Israel”, and that, “in some cases, settler violence takes place under the protection of Israeli security forces”. Perhaps the most significant development has been the shift from sanctions targeting settlers and the unofficial entities and organisations that support them towards measures directed at the settlements themselves, with Britain targeting networks that finance settlement outposts. This month, 12 Western countries, Britain, France, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, issued a joint statement describing the situation in the West Bank as “rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion”. The statement also linked these developments to the E1 project. Britain, France and Canada have announced moves towards imposing trade restrictions on settlement products, following Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium, which had previously adopted similar measures. Israel has not been able to change reality. Palestine was never a land without Palestinians, and the history of the Nakba will not be forgotten, however extensive the efforts to erase memory and conceal the documents. Nor can evidence of genocide and violations of international laws and norms be concealed for as long as the Palestinian people remain. The question today, however, is whether these responses are sufficient to deter Israel from policies, actions and crimes that have extended throughout history and afflicted an entire people across successive generations, whose cries today have become a stain on the conscience of humanity.

results.title: Five BSF personnel injured as truck turns turtle on NH-44 in Ramban
results.description: Banihal, Sep 19: Five BSF personnel were injured after a BSF truck travelling from Kashmir towards Jammu turned turtle on National Highway-44 near Chamba Seri in Ramban district on Saturday. Soon after the accident, the injured personnel were evacuated from the spot and shifted to District Hospital Ramban with the assistance of Army, police and CRPF personnel, local residents, and fellow BSF personnel. Hospital authorities said all five injured personnel were undergoing treatment. Four of them were stated to be out of danger, while the driver, Shamim Ahmed of Karnah, Kashmir, reportedly sustained serious injuries in the accident. The injured have been identified as Sunil Kumar, son of Ramesh Lal, a resident of Jammu, aged 35; Parshtum Kumar, son of Paratem Chand, a resident of Jammu, aged 36; Chandan Yadhav, son of Ravender Yadhav, a resident of Bengal, aged 38; driver Shamim Ahmed, son of Abdul Qayoom, a resident of Karnah, Kashmir, aged 38; and Sub-Inspector Ghar Singh, son of Mela Ram, a resident of Jammu. Police have taken cognisance of the incident, while further details regarding the cause of the accident are awaited.
